items.body:
Taking their cues from the 1968 silent film 'Le Révélateur', Berlin-based Hungarian-Transylvanian artist Réka Csiszér (aka VÍS) and Radwan Ghazi Moumneh (aka Jerusalem in My Heart) use synths, voices and various instruments to breathe new life into Philippe Garrel’s iconic work.

If you heard last year's grimly romantic 'Danse des Larmes', Csiszér's second VÍS album and another one-of-a-kind oddity on the always good Heat Crimes label, you might already have an inkling of how good this one's gonna be. The record was made between November 2025 and February of this year between Zurich and Montréal, where Moumneh runs the legendary Hotel2Tango studio, and it's some of the most chilling material we've heard from either artist. The duo first met in 2018 and initially debuted their soundtrack to 'Le Révélateur' live in 2023; the film had been a long-time favorite of Moumneh's, but Csiszér didn't need much convincing - its themes of displacement and disorientation made immediate sense to an artist who'd grown up with an ever-shifting idea of home, born in East Germany before moving to Vienna.

And after performing their free-flowing soundtrack a handful of times, improvising within a set of tight themes, they decided to document the project properly, borrowing a mate's house in Montréal for a few weeks to record the meat and bones. And although the baseline for the album version of the collaboration is the same ("composed through improvisation," they say), it sounds as if the themes have been weathered and lived in a little at this stage. If you've seen the film, you'll realize it's the unique mood - accentuated by Garrel's stark lighting and Michel Fournier's bold black-and-white cinematography - that carries it, and it's this high-contrast, peripatetic motion that Csiszér and Moumneh capture so magically. 

Opening track 'wahid – واحد' suggests darkness ahead with its eerie environmental sounds (creaking gates, crackly vinyl, caged birds), scraped strings and isolated synths that accompany a shot of a couple smoking in a door frame, their silhouettes cut out of the sunlight. But like the film itself, it's the juxtaposition that makes it hit; 'ithnan – اثنان' is almost celestial, an uncanny hymn made from analogue drones and soft-focus wordless voices. And when they shift into grittier territory on 'arba'a – أربعة', a short distorted instrumental that sits alongside a shot of a young boy seemingly torturing a doll, the album's long centerpiece 'khamsa – خمسة' follows it up with Csiszér's most stunning vocal performance, that lifts a long shot of the nomadic family walking down a forest road.

It's minimal but never for dull for even a moment - best viewed alongside Garrel's film for the optimum experience.

items.body:
Smacking that sweetspot between grime, techno, bassline and soca, Anthoney J Hart (East Man, Imaginary Forces) aka Basic Rhythm delivers a full-bore pack of rampers for Bristol-via-Berlin’s bassbin overlords, Sneaker Social Club.

Active in a vein of uchronic, ‘nuum-bending invention since the 2010’s, but with roots reaching back to ‘90s pirate radio, Hart’s decade-straddling steez yields the crankiest horsepower as Basic Rhythm on ‘8 Bar Techno’. Hewing hard to the brief, he dissects and recombines styles & patterns with a fiercely upfront quality, trampling on putative borders with a rudeboy alacrity that works a treat on up-for -it ‘floors.

The durable torsion of OG jungle tekno and its myriad derivations are twisted into tensile girders, variously splitting the difference between 4/4 grime and hard groove techno in ‘the title tune, or panel-beating sublow into rictus bashiness on ‘Weed Killer’, while firing killer rounds of vocal cuts including the dancehall-grime of ‘Vibez’ with NyNy, or electroid drill with Lyrical Strally and Eklipse.

Along with the precision-tooled rufige of ‘Kонец века’ with Moscow Legend, the mutant soca gallop o ‘Ice cold’, and diesel-fuelled grime-techno of ‘More Pricks than Kicks’, or the dive-bombing darkness of ‘The Deluge’, it’s a hard set for discerning 140BPM shotters, and surely one of Basic Rhythm’s deadliest.

items.body:
Produced by Neek and Jabu's Amos Childs (aka O$VMV$M), Manonmars' third album is syrupy suite of smoke-hazed recollections and free associated reflections set to decelerated, semi-rhythmic bumps, sluggish samples and cloudy drones. Sturdy biz FFO Ka, MIKE, King Vision Ultra or Coby Sey.

Manonmars' 2018 debut is one of those albums we still go back to periodically. It's that rare meeting of minds: a space for O$VMV$M to flex their production muscle and a scratchpad for London-based MC, painter and photographer Jack Martyn Richardson to sketch out his vision of England. And his experiences and impressions on 'Entertainment System' still feel chewable. "Goddess on my arm and both our phones got no service," he quips on 'Goddess'. "Acid is lysergic, psychedelic rock is Turkish." His rhymes aren't throwaway, they map out an underground that's very recognisable, shadowed by O$VMV$M's tuff, effective soundscapes - beats that reference trip-hop, ambient music, exotica and '70s movie soundtracks as much as they do US rap. On opener 'Flam3throw3r', Mars raps in double-time over shrill horns that blot out any trace of a beat; Neek and Childs sound as if they're relishing the negative space, adding chic sword swipes to a track that's got little else to do with the Wu Tang Clan. And even when a lumbering beat kicks in on 'Decathlon', flipping from downtempo to no-tempo in the final act, it sounds as if it's just there to assert O$VMV$M's commitment to slowness - Mars doesn't even seem to notice, rhyming casually but never losing his internal flow.

On 'Nasyua', his slurred expressions duck and weave around industrial whirrs and animalistic groans. "There was a time when I had flaws now I've adapted," he slurs. "I hit the zoot like Steve Zissou in 'The Life Aquatic' / then I dashed it, Christian Bale in a facemask on some Bat shit." Bristol mainstays Franco Franco and Dali de Saint Paul turn up to assist on 'Volcanic Shield', one of the album's most conventional bangers, led by O$VMV$M's skittering Surf Gang-like beats and morse code blips, and cold light's Birthmark lends his voice to 'Infinite', going bar for bar with Mars over Neek and Childs' soupy slackened funk. These moments are when 'Entertainment System' really shines, blaring out like an old tape on a busted in-car audio system. 'Firewater' takes the same approach, leaving Mars to do his best as snares are reformed into splashes alongside sultry stabs and sax from Brum-based sound artist Lorenzo Prati. "My bitch white, she can scuba dive and ice climb," he spits. "Put the drink down, I wasn't in my right mind." It's music that laughs through the tears - what could be more British than that?

items.body:
Topdown Dialectic’s solo debut bow on False Aralia rounds up over a decade of material in supremely elusive style & pattern - all rug-pulling rhythms and hallucinatory fractals wrapped up with proper, hyperreal frisson. Massive chef’s kiss FFO Vladislav Delay, Beatrice Dillon, Paperclip Minimiser, Purelink, Marc Leclair.

An artist keenly observed since initial gestures on /\\Aught in the early ‘10s, and throughout their cult LP trilogy for Peak Oil during 2018-2021; Topdown Dialectic has become a unique facet of C.21st dub electronics, adored for their grasp of diffused spatio-textural sorcery and wraithlike grooves. Anyone paying close attention to emergent sounds via Peak Oil and its False Aralia offshoot may have guessed at TD’s signature, watermarked imprint on the Borgesian Term EP of late ’25, which can now be confirmed as the work of one and the same Izaak Schlossmann; a photographer and producer patently in possession of heightened proprioceptions and a rewardingly patient approach to lushly dissociative sonification. In other words, he makes some of the sexiest electronic music out there - stuff that genuinely feels like it was made this century - and his latest practically leaves you kissing the sky thru its 80 minutes of lip-biting, skin tingling pressure. 

On 16 tracks timed at exactly 5 minutes each, we’re placed in the presence of suggestive sorcery, eliding unarchived material and jams in a unique ecology of oneiric physics. Never overtly showy or overblown, there’s nevertheless a staggering level of ingenuity and synaesthetic effect to its detailed construction and gaseous fractals resembling the LSD or DMT experience. The label themselves compare its nuance to “the flicker of a candle over a desk of drum machines in a Midwestern basement, or the “first blush of sunlight over a tiny campground as subwoofers creak in the distance”, which proves a perfectly poetic analog to its digitally-smudged refractions and tongue-tip spectral tumescence. 

Ultimately, it’s a singular pleasure to immerse the senses in Topdown Dialectic’s self-contained soundsphere, and never more substantially so than on ‘False LP A’. Longtime enthusiasts will surely recognise his skill in parsing salient aspects of Basic Channel x Rhythm & Sound, and their descendants in Vladislav Delay or Pole, reframing those templates in far more uncertain space with a real animist magick. Each work feels tangibly, ambiguously alive, breathing with dynamics and more voluminous, macro scales, and iridescent with voices and details that commands attentive listeners who will have a field day zoning in/out to its illusive, holographic projections and syncopated chronics.

items.body:
Alex Zhang Hungtai pivots yet again on 'Orion/Mother', playing (mostly) trumpet alongside some of the New York City underground scene's most intriguing improvisers, including Kwami Winfield, Laura Cocks, Lester St. Louis, TAK Ensemble's Madison Greenstone, 75 Dollar Bill's Che Chen and Leo Chang.

 'Orion/Mother' has its roots in a set of home recordings Zhang made with some of his talented local friends; "playing with you all deeply informed my current understanding in improvisation," he explains in his thank you note, "without you this album would not have existed." So over a two week period, in a rehearsal space in New York, he invited a handful of his friends to start "an ad-hoc group", playing trumpet over chopped up home recordings and wrenching them into the future. And while the finished article - split into two distinct sections - is long, it's fully worthy of your attention. As always, Zhang brings a unique ear into the room, resisting any usual improv tropes to concentrate on sounds that most artists would avoid - unruly resonances, glitches, off-piste rhythms and unsubtle interferences.

At it's best, the record sounds like jazz specters vanishing thru faded noise remnants and the wreckage of lost experiments. On 'Shadow Integration', Zhang's brassy wails echo out over a slippery, semi-rhythmic drum machine pattern, and on 'Tanhäuser Gate', the trumpet is even more isolated, weeping over a muted soundscape that's credited simply as "Ableton" on the accompanying notes. He maintains the same energy when he's working side-by-side with his collaborators, too, finding space for Winfield's circuit bent belches on 'Nataraja' and Chen and Chang's percussion on the jaw-droppingly spannered opener 'Sidewinder'. And even when the tone shifts on 'Mother', heading into a lighter (comparatively at least) zone on the woodwind-heavy 'Kali', Zhang has a knack for tying everything together with his lyrical performance. Just peep the title track, almost seven minutes of uncanny clanks and Tōru Takemitsu-strength murmurs that Zhang butters with pure improvised emotion.

items.body:
Potent, lysergic lounge music and psych-fonk-exotica out of Brussels, with Michael Crabbé letting everything slosh out of the lines in a real slow burn head melter, like Spencer Clark meets Giulio Erasmus and Pekka Airaksinen on some vintage Hoffmans. Another wyrd doozy from Antwerp’s reliably off-the-wall label, Souvenirs From Imaginary Cities.

“Straight from the weedy fields of swampville Bruxelles we bring you 8 ‘tranches de vie’ of deep zone-hall by weirdtronic bass veteran Michael Crabbé’s best fitting sound costume to date: the mighty Rudi J! You might know him from earlier outfits but that’s not the main issue here. Rudi J is!

When this swamp thing touches the pads, it’s off-road after three seconds, even if you’re in the middle of Europe’s capital. Mixing analog dirt and digital sound bits in a very loose and personal take on dancehall, we’re pretty far away from the dance floor but definitely swinging. It’s a trippy affair wandering around concrete flowers with a deep ambient flavor, but it’s edgy.

A hot summer fever dream following his own lusty path, full of life and wonder but with something sinister hiding around every corner. Often reaching for the stars, a deeper shade of bass keeps things nicely grounded. These sounds are built with a sound system in mind and bass culture at heart. Even if you can definitely surf on it from your couch, picking out all of its ear-pricking details, it will very much come alive on a big sound.

A layered affair with almost jazzy and orchestral elements peeping through the stereo-field, spectral and dissonant but also playful. Like early dubstep, some of these tunes can destroy a clubsound, keeping you skunking out in pedestrian mode and snorting up the atmospherics, finally forgetting about that damn phone.”

items.body:
The crown jewel of German duo Donna Regina's pre-Karaoke Kalk run, 'Follow the Sea' laid out the template for their best known albums, muddling electro-pop with exotica, dub and lounge and inhabiting the liminal zone between Julee Cruise and Saint Etienne.

Regina and Günther Janssen had already released three albums before 'Follow the Sea' arrived, and it was around this time that their music had begun to creep beyond Germany's borders. Matthew Herbert had issued the title track on his Lowlife imprint, bumping it up with his own remix and within a couple of years, Donna Regina had been snapped up by Karaoke Kalk, where they remained for their next umpteen full-lengths. And although each album is more or less the same, there's no other band who makes music quite like this. Regina's voice sounds pitch perfect here, calling over Günther's Kraftwerk-inspired synths on the lengthy 'Jungle' and hissing across a cheeky sample of Aphex Twin's 'Alberto Basalm' on 'Something Happy'.

It's pop music, but the kind of low-key, literate pop that no longer exists, crafted by two heads who clearly love music so much that they've been exhaustively jotting down their findings since 1992. And it's the duo's lack of consistent boundaries that keeps us coming back; they're able to lurch from dubby Americana ('Follow the Sea') to d&b ('Smile') and then try on some ritualistic 'My Life in the Bush of Ghosts' percussive experimentation - and it all sounds as if it's coming from the same honest space.

items.body:
Airbrushed, subtropical, new age ambient-jazz from Jesse Peterson’s Maui-based project, given its highest profile platform to date on Amsterdam’s Music From Memory, and warmly advised to admirers of his regular spars, Carlos Niño, Laraaji, Mia Doi Todd...

"Originally formed in New York in the late 2000s, Turn On The Sunlight has evolved into a fluid, location-spanning practice rooted in collaboration, intuition and process. Now based on Maui, Peterson’s work draws together a wide network of musicians and environments, with recordings taking shape across Los Angeles, Tokyo, London, San Miguel de Allende and Haʻikū.

Loosely situated within a framework of organic, ambient-leaning jazz, 'Iseo' unfolds as a series of open, exploratory pieces, with electronics sitting subtly beneath acoustic and environmental elements. Built from layered instrumentation including synthesizers, guitar, zither, flutes, voice and field recordings, Peterson moves between grounded, tactile detail and more expansive, immersive states. A sense of warmth and permeability runs throughout: organic percussion, environmental textures and drifting rhythmic elements lend the record a gently saturated humidity, reflecting Peterson’s base in Hawaii, where the presence of nature is felt as much as it is heard.

Underlying the project is a way of working rooted in gathering, listening and tending. Instruments, ensemble sessions, field recordings and everyday environments are approached with attentiveness, shaped through collecting, refining and allowing things to settle. Relationships, landscape and lived experience shape the sound, giving 'Iseo' a tactile, almost hand-made quality.

Rather than fixed arrangements, the album feels as if it has been organically and lovingly assembled through a process of listening and response, each element finding its place within a wider, evolving whole. This approach reaches a natural centre point in the 15-minute piece 'Medianoche En La Calle Aurora', which unfolds patiently, bending through shifting environments as motifs and textures emerge and dissolve with quiet continuity.

Peterson’s role as both instigator and facilitator is central to the project. Bringing together a diverse group of collaborators including Carlos Niño, Mia Doi Todd, Laraaji, Ko Ishikawa, Luis Pérez Ixoneztli and Miles Spilsbury, he creates space for individual voices to emerge within a shared language. The result is a music defined by openness and generosity.

'Iseo' takes its title from Peterson’s son’s middle name, a word that can be understood to mean ‘one-world life’. The piece itself takes the form of a gentle lullaby, its melody loosely shaped around the syllables of his name and sung to Peterson’s son by Luis Pérez Ixoneztli, a close collaborator whose presence across the record reflects a long-standing relationship that extends beyond the music itself.

Sleeve art and design by Michael Willis."

items.body:
Hot on the heels of their ‘Junglist!’ set, Soul Jazz reload their anthem-studded 2007 comp, packing early-mid ‘90s hardcore and ragga jungle heat by M-Beat & General Levy, Ragga Twins, SUAD, Cutty Ranks x DJ SS.

‘Rumble In The Jungle’ tells the story of jungle’s rapid evolution from mutant hip hop x dancehall in the late ’80s, via hardcore, to its hugely distinctive ragga and jump-up phase of the mid ‘90s. It’s a baga sounds that successive waves of producers have attempted to emulate ever since, but simply doesn’t get better than the OG tackle, as Soul Jazz well know.

The Ragga Twins understandably dominate the set with three bullets, the foundational, acid dancehall rap of ‘Ragga Trip’, sped-up fast rap steez of ‘Illegal Gunshot’, both from 1990, plus the ragga techno of ‘Tan So Back’ (1992), which all sparks so many dances and imaginations BITD. Shut Up and Dance, who issued all the above, are also on board, but with the gummy 2000 garage of ‘No Doubt’, which is hardly a standard, but does show how the sound had muted 10 years later.

The rest is all dead solid as a primer for inquisitive junglists/junglettes, firing General Levy’s alternative national anthem ‘Incredible’ and the murderous DJ SS remix of Cutty Ranks’ ‘Limb By Limb’, beside lesser known but wicked zingers such as DJ massive’s clattering hardcore rufige in ‘Final Conflict’, a deep fried steppa by The Source, and of course X Project’s deadly ramp of Beenie Man & Barrington Levy’s ‘Under Mi Sensi’.

Mannequin tap an arsenal of secret German electro weapons, as played by Helena Hauff and I-F, hailing a pivotal era when body music set the scene for electroclash, stuffed with zingers FFO Le Syndicat Electronique, I-F, Dopplereffekt, Drexciya, Legowelt, Adult., The Hacker, DMX Krew, Gesloten Cirkel, and early Bunker Records electro 

“Active around the turn of the millennium, both projects share the involvement of producer Ive Müller while developing distinct collaborations and approaches to electronic music. H.E.I.M. Elektronik was founded in 1996 by Holger Erlenwein and Ive Müller (after the two artists split in 1999, Müller continued using the name), while MAS 2008 is the project of Ive Müller together with René Kirchner. Though separate entities, the two projects explored a similar sonic territory: stripped-down electro, minimal electronics and machine-driven body music shaped by analog hardware and a raw DIY production ethos.

The roots of Müller’s work go back to the final years of the DDR. As a teenager he worked as a licensed DJ — officially known as a “Schallplattenunterhalter” — operating a travelling disco across Saxony. With limited access to official Western releases, music circulated through cassette recordings taped from West German radio stations such as RIAS Berlin, NDR2 and Bayern3. Together with friends he travelled between youth clubs and discos around Leipzig with a “rolling discotheque”: a Russian Wolga pulling a trailer loaded with Electro-Voice sound systems sourced through the black market.

At the turn of the 2000s this background in underground electronic culture resurfaced in a series of recordings rooted in electro, EBM and minimal machine music. The tracks collected on Electronic Corporation 2000–2002 capture this moment: cold sequences, driving rhythms and stark synthetic textures produced with a direct and uncompromising approach.

Compiled and remastered by Rude 66 from the original sources, Electronic Corporation 2000–2002 documents a small but fascinating chapter of German underground electronics from the early digital era.”

Bureau B compile stray new wave and NDW-adjacent bullets by overlooked ‘80s Austrian, Swiss, and German artists, including many making their first legit appearance.

The spiky drive and romantic melodies of early-mid ’80s Mittel European dancefloors is fully embraced on ‘Sowas von Egal 3 (German Synth Wave Underground 1981-86)’ with some 16 nuggets sifted from tape compilations and hard-to-find pressings. Prevailing streams of US & UK new wave, disco and punk are puckered with a Teutonic efficiency and wizzed-up sexiness on all counts from the bubbling hook of ‘He Sabine’ by Guyer’s Connection’ thru the DAF-esque swag of an EBM pioneer Tommi Stumpf in ‘Contergan Punk’, taking in proper club gems in Starter’s ‘Night By Night (7” Version)’, a bit of Talking Heads-like punk-funk-NDW on ‘Almenrausch’ and even Bliondie nod on ‘Die Shadocks’ ‘Disco-Liebe’. There’s some weirder robe-disco a la Felix Kubin in ‘Geduld’ by Ziggy & Eno, and a class slice of goth-rock in X-Beliebig’s ‘Morgen’.

items.body:
Following Kuboraum's eccentric 2024 first volume, the Berlin-based eyewear brand and occasional label returns with another broad-minded statement of intent featuring some of the contemporary avant-garde's most visible figures, including Low Jack, bela, Richie Culver, Rainy Miller, EROS, Lucrecia Dalt, Lee Gamble, Ziúr and Significant Other.

The set opens on a wheezing, spitting and growling loosie from bela, whose sorely overlooked 'Korean Love Sonnets' full-length is still fueling our nightmares. From there, we stay locked into the outerzone with Kuboraum vet Cosimo Damiano, an Italian techno mainstay who's veered off path in recent years, hitting SUPERPANG with his modular experiment 'Multi-Species' and helming that killer Salò record from 2023. On 'Copper Disk' he conducts an unsettling ritual, shifting voices until only ghostly outlines remain and setting the stage for similarly strong voice experiments from Marina Herlop and the unstoppable Lord Spikeheart.

Prolific French producer Low Jack shifts the mood when he invites Le Diouck to help out on the grimy, groove-fwd 'TLC' and the motion is oddly maintained by Romain Azzaro's trap-gamelan hybrid 'Fusion' and Richie Culver's rainy 'C-SIDE', that sounds as if it could have slipped off his Fixed Abode debut 'I TRUST PAIN'. What keeps us gripped here though is that while 'Kuboraum Sound Residency Vol. 2' keeps reinventing itself, it carries a similar energy throughout, an air of glam, oily darkness that links Significant Other's grinding 'Lust On Your Shoulders' with EROS's menacing 'Burnt Crossing' and Emiliano Maggi's tape dubbed lullaby 'Fury'. Softly softly does it for the gorgeous debut duo of soundtrack composer Elori Saxl & saxophonist Henry Solomon with their lushly ephemeral grasp of 4th world ambient jazz, tipped for the anyone on the line between Lynch/Badalamenti, TLF Trio, Laurel Halo, Arve Henriksen or Alex Zhang-Hungtai's Love Theme side-wind.

Captured over a few days in LA, ‘Seeing Is Believing’ frames the sax player’s searching feel for tone across soundscapes sparingly coloured in subtle harmonic gradients by Elori Saxl’s fluttering Juno 106 keys. The nine parts are testament to the duo’s near-telepathic level of intuition and mutual vision of a palpably tissue-soft atmospheric music; one where spectres of ’70s minimalism and ’80s new age bleed forward into structures equally informed by soundsystem culture and contemporary pop production, achieving a sort of slow shifting, ecological pressure system that is a pleasure to sink into.

Within her richly visual, implicitly storytelling style, Elori Saxl draws on a wellspring of experience in composing for new music ensembles, and soundtracking and directing films for New Yorker and Slate, to set spacious dimensions for Solomon’s ruminative baritone sax and bass clarinet to wander freely. A quiet sense of restraint defines proceedings as their forms gently grow and sway from the dusky licks of ‘Reverence’ thru the gauzy lustre of the title piece, conjuring a geosmin waft in ‘Raindrops’ and LA hills panorama on ‘Reno Silver’, or balmiest breeze of Glass-like phrasing on ‘A Thousand Steps’, into the gorgeous, pitch bent and sensual sorcery summoned in standout ‘Heart.’

Stunner.

Ghost Dubs & The Bug duppy the latter’s cult, isolationist ambient excursion of 2022 with apposite measures of lead-boot trod and atmospheric levity for the hardest-to-please industrial dub freaks.

Selected cuts from ’Sub Zero’ - Kevin Richard Martin’s concerted return to interests in ambient-dub-noise fundamentals - are robustly togged out with bass insulation and Goretextured to the elements for a supremely crushing session that benefits from the biggest speakers you can lay yr mitts on. It catches KRM arguably in his imperial phase, sustaining a tear of substantial gear penned under his own name since ‘Sirens’ (Room 40, 2019) deep into the belly of his sound, to now clasp these chiral aspects of his steez - the supine, sunken, and strongback, stepping - in a deathly bind.

KMR’s key spar and Pressure MVP, Ghost Dubs goes super dank and wide on his half, opening subterranean caverns of space below ‘When I’m Gone’, punctuated only by abandoned ice-breaker clank and timber-shiver chorales, before pushing leagues below into knackered Porter Ricks or Rhythm & Sound terrain on rework of ‘Sorrow’. Martin keeps up his end of the bargain with a sonorous diffusion of ‘Screwed’, all icy plangency and keeling bass recalling aspects of Mika Vainio’s ‘Kilo’, then plumbing guttural crevasses of the spirit on remix of ‘Too Human’.

Nkalipho Andile Mkhize aka Akiid blazes thru with 11 sharp sidespins on gqom, ama & Afrotech, inflected with Jersey club, trance, trap and techno - all demonstrating why he’s one of Durban’s rising stars.

‘Skeffu’ hustles some of the hottest strains of harder-edged club and street rave emerging from South Africa in the mid 2020s. The distinct sound speaks to Akiid’s peripatetic youth, moving between Durban townships where he picked up myriad local styles and patterns which fed into his rudely mutable and robustly disciplined sound. Call it gqom 2.0, hybrid Afrotech, or the Future Sound of Durban; whatever, it’s properly effective dance music certain to catch fire far beyond the source.

Fierce from front to back, ‘Skiffu’ is emblematic of the way SA artists absorb virulent sounds into their very particular dance vernacular. A youthful zeal for the thrills of contemporary Black Atlantic sounds - Jersey club, ATL trap, Chi & LDN drill - is factored by production techniques from megadome EDM, dub techno and even psytrance, to generate a ceaseless FWD traction in its pointed limb/limbic triggers. It’s all there in the breathless tension of ‘Chuck Norris’ and most impressive on the sound design staging of ‘MoonWalk Two’, where Jersey drill-type bass and an almost Burial-esque woodblock ushers detuned, mentasm-like licks to a heart-in-mouth breakdown.

As with any style, it’s possible to reach a point of saturation or exhaustion before the ears reach overfamiliarity and seek new thrills, and its maybe fair to say gqom hasn’t offered all that much that’s new in recent times (or at least that we’ve caught on to). But Akiid’s lust for fresh pressure, as heard on the angler canter of the title track, or his chimeric Jersey club x trance stabbed with isiZulu calls and scratch motifs in ‘Emotional Damage’, acutely remedy that issue with a thrilling, recombinant sense of club dramaturgy.

TIP!

A second pressing of last year’s gorgeous fourth and final album from Old Saw, the American Primitive project of Tongue Depressor's Henry Birdsey, riffing on the classic Takoma paradigm with additional ferric washes and layered instrumental drones, huge recommendation if yr into Bruce Langhorne’s ‘The Hired Hand’ or classic work by Daniel Lanois, Laraaji, Pelt, Stars Of The Lid, State River Widening.

'The Wringing Cloth' is Birdsey’s fourth and final Old Saw outing, and ironically it’s also the one that has garnered most amount of critical and commercial success. Old Saw’s shimmering, drone-heavy soundscapes were recorded on 1/4" tape at various locations in New England over the last few years and are once again paired with evocative black and white imagery from photographer Dylan Hausthor, whose landscapes somehow perfectly capture the timeless, widescreen appeal of the music inside.

Birdsey's pedal, lap steel and resonator are at the core of each track, but the album also features Old Saw’s usual personnel; Harper Reed on nylon string guitar and banjo, Ira Dorset on fiddle and bowed strings, Ann Rowlis on reed organ and harmonium, Jim Cutler on telecaster, Addison Starkweather-Price on bass, and Peter Catchpole on metal objects and power hammer. That lap steel lends the music its stylistic anchor, taking us through decades of American folk before gently fraying at the edges. Birdsey's application of classical minimalism - the themes that surge through his work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor - is still somehow present here, especially as the record pulls into its second side and the shimmering country-fied atmosphere is pierced with bell-like sounds, but the overall mood and flavour of the record is distinctly easy on the ear and timeless in its appeal.

As the label put it, “What has always been uncanny about this music is that it arrives in a state at once familiar and obscured, like a memory weighed down with sensory information but no identifying details to place it. The Wringing Cloth walks off further into that geographical dream without time or language, until it’s just a speck of light….”

In other words, high praise!

items.body:
Modular bod M. Geddes Gengras gets the band back together on 'Guestlist', roping in an estimable team of collaborators (including Christina Carter, WANDA GROUP, Greg Fox, Ben Chasny and Meg Duffy, among others) to recapture the lightning in a bottle energy of Chicago's early post-rock era, when sounds would criss-cross over each other relatively freely.

Despite technology being accessible, commonplace even, it's still relatively difficult to find the sweet spot between live instrumentation and electronics. Modular synthesis, that thrives on its self-contained, often unpredictable moments of serendipity, adds an even more problematic element. You can make it work, sure, but so much of what we like about modular music is that it doesn't feel as if it's been looped into structures that file down its sharp edges. Gengras sets himself a challenge here, working like a synthesist but also drawing on his experience playing in bands - he sees both sides, which gives him a head-start. And he's also got the good sense to think back to an era where the possibilities felt endless: the "early Pro Tools" era as James Toth writes in the accompanying notes, when bands like Tortoise and The Sea and Cake were looking at artists like Autechre and AFX and wondering what techniques they could integrate.

And 'Guest List' is undoubtedly Gengras' most ambitious record to date. There's more to it than personnel, too - proper songs, a far cry from the hazy new age-tinted synth jams that we heard on 'Expressed, I Noticed Silence' or the post-kosmische "ROMpler worship" of 'QUIK-MELT', appear in the dense tangle of instruments and expressions. While the 11-minute 'The List is Millions Long' initially seems to not-so-subtly reference Tortoise's 'Millions Now Living...' with its chiming guitars and motorik beat (supplied by Portland-based sound artist Colin Blanton, no less), it gets more complicated when Will Epstein's saxophone enters the frame. And that harmonic complexity remains when the track melts into 'Laplace/Montagne' and Gengras' synth belches are augmented by Chasny's golden shreds. Hell, there are even vocals on 'Seven Dials' provided by Austin's Cory Plump, who shouts listlessly over Gengras' sunny arpeggios, Fox's drums and Duffy's riffs.

Prepare yourself, 'Guest List' is not the M. Geddes Gengras you're likely to be expecting. There's even a spoken word intro to the album's brilliant finale '"The Weather"' from cult social media star and sometime genius WANDA GROUP. Proper good.

Balinese gamelan master Dewa Alit's third Black Truffle outing, 'Baur Bentur' continues to shake up the formula like it's a margarita, placing Alit's Gamelan Salukat ensemble alongside virtuoso jazz pianist Sri Hanuraga.

With each of Alit's Black Truffle albums, his first releases outside of Indonesia, the performer, composer, instrument designer and bandleader has projected Balinese gamelan forms into bold new places. 2020's 'Genetic' set the scene, introducing his orchestra and his uniquely tuned scale and its follow-up, 2022's 'Chasing the Phantom' considered gamelan's immense influence on electronic music, centering some of Alit's most experimental material. On 'Baur Bentur', which means "mixing and smashing", Alit again looks at the push-and-pull between East and West, this time wondering how to work out a fusion that's progressive, not something formulated around the gaze of parasitic tourists. He invites Jakarta-born Hanuraga to help him realize this goal and its a sensible choice; considered one of Indonesia's most talented young pianists, Hanuraga understands both avant-garde jazz and traditional Indonesian music implicitly. 

His playing is measured but ornate on 'Sukat Tacara', played in fast flurries of notes that recall gamelan without mimicking the form. It allows Alit's ensemble to take a different approach, laying down hollow rhythms at first and slow chimes before speeding up into more traditional overlayed, lightning-fast tones in the middle section. And it's at this moment that Hanuraga really steps into the spotlight, playing jerky Thelonius Monk-style sequences that mutate seamlessly into cascading gamelan riffs. The title track on the flip takes a different approach again, integrating Hanuraga's piano more holistically into the ensemble, where it follows the gamelan's rhythmelodic thrust absolutely, adding emphasis, accent and intrigue to a sound that's already exceptionally singular.

Necessary re-up of a near 50 year old Afrobeat ace led by Fela’s regular sax blower, featuring Fela on keys, in the pendulous ‘Low Profile’ and a rework of Afrobeat anthem ‘Se Rere’ future-proofed by its slink trot...

“After years touring the world as Fela’s baritone saxophonist, Animashaun stepped forward to lead the legendary Egypt 80 band following Tony Allen’s departure, remaining the group’s musical director until Fela’s death in 1997. He continued on subsequent tours with Seun Kuti until 2016. Lekan began recording his only solo project, Low Profile, in 1977. The album was composed and recorded across sessions at home in Nigeria and on tour with Fela, who both produced the recordings and added keyboards to the album’s title track.

‘Low Profile (Not For The Blacks)’ referenced a government campaign during the country’s 1970s oil boom: “It was inspired by a speech by Olusegun Obasanjo, Nigeria’s military Head of State, when he urged black people to keep a low profile about their wealth and not to behave in a vulgar, arrogant way,” explains Lekan. “I argued that low profile is not just for the blacks, as everyone is human, regardless of race.” On the flip side, the simmering Afrobeat anthem ‘Se Rere’ (which translates as ‘Do Right’) delivers Animashaun’s message of living with integrity: do right, and you will reap what you sow. The song later became the band’s opening number during Fela’s live performances both in Nigeria and internationally throughout the 1980s and ’90s.

Despite recording beginning almost two decades earlier, Low Profile did not receive an official release until 1995, when it finally surfaced on Fela’s Kalakuta label. One of only a handful of albums led by core members of Kuti’s band, Low Profile captures a pivotal moment in Afrobeat history. Over time, the original has become a rare and highly sought-after record, and this new reissue places the spotlight back on a modest but influential Nigerian legend.

Strut’s reissue features the complete original artwork, is fully remastered by The Carvery, and includes brand new liner notes by Lekan Animashaun himself.”

items.body:
Performed by Balinese gamelan duo KADAPAT and Indonesian singer and musician Nova Ruth Setyaningtyas, 'Ocean Cage' is a live recording of Asiandopeboys latest performance 'Moyang & Seaman', a collaboration with choreographer Siko Setyanto that draws from Japanese Noh theater and Nusantara traditions.

If you've been paying attention, you'll already know that anything with Tianzhuo Chen's name on it is worthy of a closer look. And Chen is in the director's chair on 'Ocean Cage', fusing installation art, choreography, live music and scenography into a brand new Asiandopeboys theatrical extravaganza that's almost predictably ambitious. The show is pegged to a narrative that's inspired by Indonesian whaling traditions and local legends, focusing on three characters that Setyanto interprets to build an allegorical account of displacement and ecological collapse. But the interesting part for those of us who aren't able to check into one of the shows is that the music is gripping even without the visuals; KADAPAT approach gamelan traditions with a refreshing level of irreverence, using electronic instruments as well as the traditional bamboo and metal tools to mash up the timeline, not exactly fusing gamelan elements with far-off templates but rethinking the form in situ. 

Their tonal clusters and rhythmic experiments are aptly meshed with Nova Ruth's powerful vocals, that sail across the soundtrack, sometimes squeezed into an unsettling robotic moan and oftentimes left to soar on its own. She grew up in Java and spent seven years traveling on the solar-powered boat Arka Kinari, a "floating cultural platform to sound the alarm on climate change." So the music sounds as if it's plugged into a reality that gets more stark each year; there's a sense that 'Ocean Cage', although it's steeped in ancient traditions, is being beamed from the future, a warning of where the world is headed if we don't do something immediately. It's beautiful, of course, but it's sobering too.

Following her acclaimed 2022 album 'Weather Alive', Beth Orton returns with another fully self-produced collection of songs, this time bringing in help from Shahzad Ismaily, Vernon Spring's Sam Beste, drummers Chris Vatalaro and Vishal Nayak, trumpet player Christos Styliandes and bassist Tom Herbert.

Orton sounded refreshed on 'Weather Alive'. Taking the production into her own hands for the first time, she crafted a personal world that was completely her own, weaving in old recordings of her parents and recording a busted piano she snapped up at Camden Market. The music felt like a form of catharsis, dreamily reflecting on years of boozing and raving, when she made her mark as a guest vocalist for artists like the Chemical Brothers and William Orbit. That mature, knowing air - the kind of mettle you build up only after real-world experience - hangs around 'The Ground Above', giving Orton's tender, heartfelt songs genuine power and proper weight. When she sings "I'm as invincible as grief, dancing cross a lake of loss," on the epic opener 'The Ground Above', you don't doubt her for a moment.

Orton's voice has always been distinct, a soulful rasp that's fragile one moment and sturdy the next, and it sounds as if she's finally found the right music to match it. On that eight-minute opener, it's quick syncopated drums that lodge themselves somewhere between Roni Size's 'New Forms' and Radiohead's 'Hail to the Thief', reversed, psychedelic guitar riffs, jazzy horn blasts and pillowy ambient textures. 'Cigarette Curls', meanwhile, slows things down, pairing her voice with smudged piano phrases and smoke-y rhythms. She breezes past the shape of classic soul pop on 'Waiting', even taking on a half-sung chorus, but sounds most comfortable when she strips down the instrumentation even further, crooning over brushed percussion and euphoric pads on the gorgeous 'I'll Miss You'.

One decade since minting the ‘Long Trax’ series on Terre Thaemlitz’s label, Comatonse, Will Long slow cooks six new additions on his personal folio, taking all the time needed to get right into the groove. Trust there’s no fireworks or over-produced trickery, just hypnotic deep house that unfurls with a real sense of space, patience and deferred gratification.

Long in his element, following his nose to pair the barest ingredients in classic style and pattern, as with with the likes of ‘About Where It's At (Now You Went N' Did It mix)’, which takes over 4 mins happily swinging away before introducing its lonesome flute motif, or a standout ‘Have to Have Something’ lost in the flow, where the bassline only thickens as it goes along. 

We’re also partial to the square bass budge of ‘Have To Have Something (S' a Lotta Shade mix)’, and the mesmerising meld of creamy bass and piquant cowbell pinging on ‘The Problems’, also found warped with trippier effect on its Metallic Dub reshape.

alias Junior Rain are the duo of sound poet Francesco Cavaliere and sound artist Matteo Martino, minting Turin’s Isotopes Records with a tape of exquisitely heatsick wooze tipped FFO Spencer Clark, Jan Jelinek, Lieven Martens, NWAQ, Actress, Rezzet...

‘Capello di Cristallo’ could hardly be a more fitting soundtrack to the head-melting heatwave right now. For just shy of 30 mins, Cavaliere dials down his signature sound poetry to instrumental form, matched by Matteo Martino’s ear for textural, world-building detail, as previously revealed on his tape for ace DIY label Canti Magnetici. Across 11 works, the duo transcend the sum of their influences; whiffs of rearview vaporwave and new age ambient entwine around impulses from lo-fi Midwestern house, and its Euro offshoots, in a treacle-thick air oozing with ferric wow & flutter that sounds custom-made for high heat.

Subtly distinguished from Cavaliere’s decades of work by its slow burning rhythms, the album sways to its own dreamy pace thru pieces that melt into one another. The silvery chord bursts and busted drums of ‘in discesa’ feel like a knackered Sun Ra, and ‘espansione’ incurs Raul Lovisoni & Francesco Messina’s Cramps touchstone, hinting at a spiritual ambient jazz freeness that also colours their titular vacillation of lo-fi house, and the Rezzett-esque romance in ‘junior rain’ or ‘ragnelata magica’. 

Consider it a compliment to the artists that if you reach the end of the spool in an eyes-half-closed, bezonked state, their work here is done.

A parody of Brian Eno's 'Music for Airports' recorded at the heart of a banana plantation in Tenerife, Lagoss's 'Música para Plátanos' (music for bananas) is anything but background music, fixing up its ratcheting polyrhythms and "Latin-infused electronics" with flimsy exotica and oddball environmental recordings.

The music of 'Música para Plátanos' isn't just about the plantation, it attempts to live, breathe and exist just like the bananas themselves, reacting to each element whether it's the temperature or the nourishment. And the tracks came together over weekly improvised sessions recorded over the space of five years, where the trio of Gonçalo F. Cardoso, Mladen Kurajica and Daniel Baez tapped into their groove, fusing samples and tape loops with shifting percussive forms, instrumental outbursts and radio interference. If you heard 2024's 'Plátano Tapes', you'll have a good idea where the source of this record came from, but that collage has been worked into, shaved down, shaped and refined since then, distilled as a "greatest rotten hits" according to the press release, for an album that's meant to be distinct from their ongoing 'Imaginary Island Music' series.

It's good stuff, too, more engaging than you'd expect from a collection of jams, but then Lagoss are a force to be reckoned with. There's horizontal exotica - the organ-led 'Mundo Sour' and the skittering 'Plata no Police' - and plenty of oily ambient biz (just check 'Milliones de Gallinas'), but Lagoss are best when they're in a percussive groove. On 'Mosca Blanca / Horcón Girl', they muddle field recordings with low-slung bassy grooves and circuitous island rhythms, and 'Plátano Saki' is Tenerife in dub, a banana-themed, sun-bleached anthem that's seasoned with tape echo, reverb and manic Lee "Scratch" Perry-esque oscillations.

The second ever public performance by Nurse With Wound, captured on tape in 1984 and held in Steven Stapleton's archive across the four decades since, now available on a vinyl edition for the first time - every copy painted by hand, edition of 300.

You get the measure of this one with Steven Stapleton’s assertion that this was less a gig and more a “series of confrontations with audiences who often had no idea what they were watching.” which is basically everything we hope for watching pretty much anything.

It belongs to a moment when Stapleton, working alongside collaborators including David Tibet, Andrew McKenzie of The Hafler Trio, and a rotating cast of percussionists and string players, was carrying NWW briefly out of the studio. The performance moves through the territory NWW had been mapping across Homotopy to Marie and Nature Unveiled: long passages of pre-recorded tape collage assembled by Stapleton and McKenzie, ridden over by live electronics, voice, percussion, and a surreal theatrical instinct.

or as the band call it, “a collective groping”

aye.

Referencing Van Dyke Parks, Robert Wyatt and Jim O'Rourke, Los Angeles' Aaron MF Olsen goes full chamber pop on his second "songs for singing" album.

Olsen keeps himself busy. In the last few years, he's penned a raft of scores (including one for Matt Hewitt's bizarre b-movie 'Hoagie'), worked alongside Jeff Parker and interpreted Mexican singer-songwriter José Alfredo Jiménez's classing songs on synthesizer. And he's also written two albums of proper songs: 2021's acclaimed 'Songs Album' and this impressive sequel, that's comprised of 10 well sculpted baroque pop moments, each one fleshed out by Olsen's band.

He's not quite as ambitious as Cindy Lee or Panda Bear, but there are moments when Olsen shows a similar command of past, present and future. As the throwbacky 'Nobody Can Tell' fades out, 'There Comes A Time' enters the frame in a brush of looped noise and synth euphoria before settling into its groove, and 'Who Do You Think You Are I Am?' is a minimal throb of staccato percussion and detuned piano hits that rights itself mid-way through when it transforms into a low-slung doo-wop anthem.

items.body:
Capturing an in-situ rehearsal of The Sterling Jubilee Singers, a long-running African American a cappella quartet, 'Jesus Hits like the Atom Bomb' provides an intimate view of a dying folk tradition.

We should all know by now the foundational influence African American gospel music has had on subsequent popular forms, from country to house, but we rarely get to hear the real thing. This set was produced by the Alabama Folklife Association and aimed to document the rigorous process the Sterling Jubilees went through each week to maintain their notoriously high level of activity. The group was formed way back in 1929 from African American miners and mill workers in Birmingham, Alabama, and 'Jesus Hits...' catches up with them in 1994 in a hall that serendipitously sat next to a railway line. And whether you have any interest in OG gospel a cappella music or not, it's fascinating to hear the quartet in their element, praying in-between recreating their elaborate (and impeccably sung) set of standards. It's a porthole into another universe, for those of us who grew up far from the American South.

items.body:
Finally, Kompakt issue a true GAS outlier on vinyl for the first time, recorded in 1989 and containing some of Wolfgang Voigt’s earliest and starkest recycling of magisterial Wagner loops, closest to the ends of The Caretaker, Philip Jeck, Kevin Drumm.

One of those releases that has lurked on our shelves since 2008 as a book and CD, ‘November 89’ exists in the margins of Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS canon as its creepiest and most occluded evocation of long walks in the Bavarian forests. While other GAS classics ooze a sort of dappled warmth breaking thru the trees in their widescreen dub techno strolls, you can fully feel the light dying over the horizon and the forest drawing in on this particularly gloomy, hour-long suite. 

As the title suggests, it was mostly, remarkably, made in ’89, back when Voigt was finding his feet between techno, house and indie-pop, and nearly a decade before he co-founded Kompakt with Michael Mayer & Jürgen Paape - by which time he was a full-fledged rave dynamo as Love Inc. and myriad others notable projects. And, in that sense, it can be heard as his ‘Selected Ambient Works 89-95’ - or perhaps more pertinently with SAW II vibes - in his nascent attempt to chase the ambient dragon, which surely endures for its strangely nostalgic, unheimlich qualities.

An educated guess leads us to think the first three were made in ’89, taking in the nightfall scenery of smudged symphonic strings and icy crackle to ‘Der Wald’, plus the muddied bass waltz and spectral pall of ‘Das Moor’, thru the self-evidently titled centrepiece ‘1989-11-01’, bristling with a digitally iridescent dread. ‘Tal 90’ and ‘Nah Und Fern’, which shares its title with the 2008 boxset, were most likely made a little later, and find the wintry doom thawing to the GAS-eous forms we’ve all come to deeply know and adore. 

A true evergreen for deep ambient techno connoisseurs, no less

An advanced masterclass in Berlin beat science, ‘Wireless’ is the final and arguably strongest solo release by T++; aka Torsten Pröfrock, an artist with a long lineage of important releases under numrous aliases - Dynamo, Erosion,Log, Resilent, Traktor, Various Artists and more - a true pillar of Berlin's Techno legacy.

First issued by Honest Jon’s in 2010, the 2x12” features samples of singer and ndingidi-player Ssekinomu (originally found on the EMI archival dive ‘Bellyachers, Listen - Songs From East Africa, 1938-46’) reworked by Pröfrock into a volley of rambunctious but rudely disciplined club workouts some 75 years later. In many other hands, this could have been just another passable cut ’n splice edit, but T++ treats the material with a balance of reverence and raving license, highlighting an instinctive understanding of the original music's intent and purpose, and their deep rooted connection to modern fast rap and hardcore dance musics.

The four tracks amount to a contemporary classic in their field and also exist in a strong tradition of German artists ranging from Stockhausen to Can and Basic Channel whose music has crucially incorporated the fluid, rolling nature and spectra of African drumming patterns. However, it’s vital to point out that T++’s take on African drumming is also filtered thru a love of UK music - Jungle, D&B, garage, dubstep - meaning that his rhythms are properly underlined with syncopated, technoid basslines owing as much to Kingston, Jamaica as Brixton and Sheffield in the UK.

For anyone who had been intently listening to Pröfrock's output since his Traktor gems, thru his Dynamo aces, to early work with Monolake and his string of seminal T++ 12”s in the 2000’s, on its release in 2010 ‘Wireless’ quickly came to epitomise his approach to broken techno production at its most open-ended and inexorable. Between the itchy, sprung step of ‘Cropped’, the puckish darkside torque of ‘Anyi’, a voodoo communal in ‘Voice No Bodies’, and the reanimated spirits of ‘Dig’ you have some of the finest mutant techno ever cut to vinyl.

An absolute must-have for dancers and DJs.

Abstract dub dream-weavers SKRS INTL. & WZRDRY remerge at the behest of Bristol’s Accidental Meetings for a super lush dose of wormholing ambient dance pressure tipped FFO Rezzett, Peak Oil/False Aralia, Second Woman.

‘Orbit Flares’ combines the two Canadian units for the first time in over a decade, naturally reprising an empathic level of vibes in a half hour of music that betrays illusive tekkerz developed over the interim. Any semblance of sharp edges are smudged to a brilliantly psychedelic, polychromatic lustre and laced with disciplined, yet properly wayward rhythms that tumble, buckle and vaporise in fractious delirium. Each new SKRS drop is welcome around ours but, jeez, they really push into their most impressive work here, possibly thanks to wzrdryAV’s synaesthetic suss.

Front to back it feel likes they catch minds/bodies in the split second before going under anaesthesia, and extrude us into pitch-bent helical vortices of plonging dub chords and gooey bass, finding bold new realms of computerised dub suss. Handrails are slippery as fuck, ground melts beneath feet, leaving bodies gyring in space between the weightless dub techno inflections of ‘1.1’, into air-stepping chicanery on ‘1.2’, or glitching like a hair-kissing Vladislav Delay on ‘1.3’. The smeared chords and scudding subs of ‘2.1’ call to mind Second Woman emulating the illusive dub-soul of False Aralia drops, and ‘2.3’ feels like distant rig heard on a Nitrous-induced permo. 

Sheer class for harder to please future dub freaks.

Featuring MØ, Quiet Light, Koilwood, Helena Gao and others, Copenhagen duo A Good Year's second album is another slick set of trip-hop inspired Danish pop from the reliable Escho stable, home of Smerz, Astrid Sonne, Iceage and Snuggle.

Albert Hildebrand and Tobias Laust Hansen didn't have a fixed idea in mind when they started work on 'Play'. As the title suggests, it emerged from just playing, improvising with each other and shuttling recordings back and forth between their collaborators. "The music became a vessel for connection," they explain. "A way to reach to people we admire, but also a way to create a social element within these sometimes introverted jams." And their approach leads to an uncommonly light set of almost-pop; it's still as neatly polished as anything from the fertile Copenhagen scene, but there's a willing naivety that allows breathing room, a way for errors to slip in and humanize the material in the face of AI perfection.

Fine collaborator Koilwood shows up on the charming 'Back of a car', whispering softly over Hildebrand and Hansen's skipping lo-fi beats and skeletal instrumentation and Tiffi Malmgren lends her voice to early highlight 'Flight', a slo-mo trip-hop dream that's lifted by the duo's tape-warped piano vamps and hazy textures. And Malmgren returns with Major Lazer collaborator MØ (yep it was her on 'Lean On') on the album's stand-out 'Blue Flame', an electrified indie anthem that makes good use of the Danish singers' unique, recognizable voices. Scandi pop lovers, this'll hit the spot.

Released in 2017, Dasein was Richard H. Kirk's first solo album in 5 years, recorded by the founding member of Cabaret Voltaire at Western Works, Sheffield, over a three-year period.

"Work began with recording on midi and analogue synthesisers before guitar and vocals (Kirk’s first use of vocals in 10 years) were added. Kirk explains, “A lot of time was spent on post-production, editing and then living with the material and I think it benefited from stepping back and then revisiting after doing other things.”

Although not an overtly political album, it’s hard not to hear a reaction to recent years’ world events in the overwhelming urgency of ‘Nuclear Cloud’ or ‘20 Block Lockdown’ or in ‘New Lucifer / The Truth Is Bad’. When questioned Kirk admits, “It’s not really a political album, but over recent years – during the recording – all manner of horrorshow events have cropped up and now we seem to be in a rerun of the Cold War with Russia back as the Bogeyman.” The album’s title, Dasein (a German word meaning “being there” or “presence”, often translated into English as “existence”), is a fundamental concept in existentialism.

Kirk explains “culture succumbs to nostalgia in much the same way that an individual looks back wistfully to adolescence or childhood - the nostalgia is partly for a time when he or she wasn’t nostalgic, just lived purely IN THE NOW.” In 2014, during the recording period, Kirk began work on Cabaret Voltaire live and so the two projects coexisted in tandem. Although Kirk’s varied projects have always existed separate to one another, says Kirk, “in the past some solo works served as a blueprint for what I did later with Cabaret Voltaire”.

Billed as a performance consisting solely of machines, multi-screen projections and Richard H. Kirk, Cabaret Voltaire recently announced the first UK performance in over 20 years at the Devil’s Arse Cave (aka Peak Cavern) in Castleton, Derbyshire on Saturday 29 April. Kirk will perform entirely new material for a performance relevant to the 21st Century with no nostalgia."

Prayers are answered with Vainqueur’s Reductions 1995-1997, a compilation of in-demand cuts from René Löwe’s seminal Chain Reaction 12”s and Elevations CD, including the vinyl premiere of Antistatic and first ever appearance of Antistatic II on any format, all available on wax for the first time in years.

For anyone who came thru during the late ‘90s and early ‘00s, Vainqueur records were it - providing some of the strongest dub techno in existence. Now, three decades later, their influence probably looms larger than ever.

To newcomers and fiends alike, this 3LP selection provides a perfectly formed overview of Vainqueur’s most feted period (not withstanding his all-time banger Lyot [1992], but that was a kinda one-off). The first disc revolves around the banging Reduce 1 and the monotone brilliance of Reduce 2, whilst the 2nd renders the more tender gasps and dub chords of Solanus (Original) and the heady Elevation II - both masterclasses in techno minimalism - while the 3rd disc significantly presents the flared chords of Antistatic, taken from the Elevations CD, on vinyl for the 1st time, backed with the exclusive-to-this-12” Antistatic II.

Unmissable.

items.body:
A rare window into Angolan musical culture. Guitarist Mário Rui Silva folds traditional Angolan and West African rhythms into European jazz forms, creating music that's subtle, beautiful and completely distinct. 

'Stories from Another Time' compiles music from three of Silva's 1980s albums, "Sung’Ali", "Tunapenda Afrika" and "Koizas dum Outru Tempu". Silva was a researcher and intellectual who was motivated to find the roots of Angolan culture in spite of its centuries-long struggle with colonization. Spurred on by Angolan musical legend Liceu Vieira Dias of traditional band Ngola Ritmos, Silva wanted to understand the politics and spiritualism behind Angolan music. Dias took traditional semba and kazukuta rhythms and infused them into contemporary music in the '40s and '50s, helping Angola to find national pride as the country struggled to assert itself after years of colonial rule.

Luanda-born Silva attempted to do similar with his music - and while it sounds aesthetically similar to Brazilian music of the 1970s, this was almost accidental. Silva was in fact attempting to move away from Portugese-centered culture and its tropical fetishism, and develop a sound that was purely Angolan. The music is hard to place, it sounds almost out of time, both ancient and surprisingly contemporary, with soft pop hooks underpinned by complex polyrhythms and chiming mbira. The fusion feels fluid and considered - there's no cynicism here at all, rather Silva approaches his sounds with a deft, open-hearted charm that rings from every word and lightly-picked note. Huge recommendation.

100% killer reissue of Bim Sherman’s self-released 1988 dub masterpiece ‘Ghetto Dub’, mixed by King Tubby, Prince Jammy and Adrian Sherwood who diffuse rhythms by The Roots Radics and Sly & Robbie, newly remastered for its first new edition in 30 years.

With 2nd hand prices understandably climbing into triple figures, this overdue first vinyl reissue will be mana to the fiends. It takes pride of place in an ongoing programme of resurrected Sherman aces to portray him at his most elusive and atmospheric, or as the hype sticker calls it, “a journey in echo and space”.

His legendarily tone is threaded thru the desk by a team of JA/UK titans with the man himself in the producer role, sifting cuts from his Century Records: a label set up in the Uk in 1984, after his move from Kingston, JA, to London, where he became a crucial figure in the On-U Sound crew after joining their 1979 tour, and would lend to classic Dub Syndicate cuts among others. 

The record’s renown has grown over the years since Sherman’s passing in 2000 and the effective dissolution of his label. Week-End Records now do a sterling job of preserving his legacy with this edition, richly representing the warmth and pressure of the OG in its entirety, from the clean-spurred, buoyant step of its title tune to moon-booted ‘Untitled Dub’, via the soul-tugging ace ’Station Dub’ with its unanswered doorbells, and best showcase of his voice in ‘Moving Dub’, another alright stepper in ‘World Dub’, the bloozy wooze of ‘Danger Dub’ and wickedly skewed Afro-lilt of ‘Tribulation Dub.’

All killer.

Drawing on his experiences in Ghana, Niamké Désiré approaches his third record with a different energy, infusing his productions with noise and chaos to offset the fragile beauty of his work with violinist ASIA. RIYL Kevin Martin, Tim Hecker, Shapednoise or Ben Frost.

Describing his recent trip to Ghana as "an overwhelming, magnificent organization of noise," Désiré returned to Paris determined to shake up his methodology. He's already proven himself on albums like 2021's 'Simulacrum', 2023's 'Rhizomes' and last year's 'Ego Death' collaboration with Resina to be a prodigious sound designer and deep thinker, but he realised that it was stepping outside of his head that was needed. So, thinking about the journey rather than the destination, Désiré began to work on music with violinist ASIA for a Parisian commission that was more assertively personal, considering the actual feeling of "diasporic in-betweenness" he experienced as he moved between Paris and Ghana, rather than speculating on philosophy. The result was '100 Soleils', a lengthy composition that Désiré splits into four pieces on 'The Sun Turned Black', using it as a blueprint for the feel of the entire record. 

Threaded through with ASIA's delicate string work, Désiré's newfound confidence in noise evolves over the course of almost half an hour, giving Désiré's competent sound design the fangs it needed. There's natural chaos to the soundscape he creates on '100 Suns, Pt. II', animalistic screeches that complement his digitally-shaped elements, and we begin to sense an interplay between very different worlds. Désiré creates the same friction between the electronic and acoustic instrumentation, building vast artificial melodic structures on the towering '100 Suns, Pt. III' and resolving them on the fourth chapter with ASIA's sweeping strings. Breaking up the piece, 'The Children of Noise' establishes dissonance and the title track acts as a brief, gratifying conclusion, finding harmony between the desiccated, buzzing noise and Désiré's richly textured harmonic clouds.

items.body:
'Aeternum (Existenz)' from Dave Sumner, aka Function on Tresor. 

"Much like the fusion resulting in the output of light and heat within a star, the last seven years for Dave Sumner, aka Function, have been defined by immense change and an outpouring of creative energy. What began in late 2016 as a period of burnout from a relentless touring life became a catalyst for the most prolific recording era of his career. At the time, the studio became the only viable escape, a space to transmute exhaustion into a gestalt work.

Aeternum (Existenz) serves as the missing element in this creative arc. It acts as the final chapter of a cycle, that began with the 2019 album Existenz and moved through Subject f (Transcendence), Awakening from the Illusory Self, and Green EP. Drawing inspiration from the seven stages of alchemy, this mini-album represents a cathartic process; a natural end point of a psychological cycle and the beginning of a new curve.

Across the six tracks on the mini-LP, recorded 2016-2019, Function builds a unique world, one which underlines his place as one of the luminaries of contemporary techno.

Opening track, Ascent, traverses the space between ambient and techno; second track City Of Luz almost fades into itself across its twelve minutes before Transmutation brings around a reawakening with a beat that would not have sounded out of place on an early Rephlex or even a Sähko release. Final track on the 12”, Growth Cycle is fittingly a re-version/re-vision of a track on the Existenz LP; Robert Owens’ soulful vocal now Stefanie Parnow's floating Siren-like voice with music that feels reborn: fresh, strong and insistent.

The digital pack contains two further tracks, the deep electro of November 29, as well as Rubedo, a spacial ambient track that feels like the final glowing red embers of a fire turning to ash as the sun rises to reveal a new, golden dawn.

Aeternum (Existenz) is the final chapter of the soundtrack to Function’s spiritual awakening, the closing of a door and the clearing of a path. It’s a sonic manifestation of the Magnum Opus completed, a moment of total integration, where the leaden weight of the journey is finally perfected into the incorruptible gold of the spirit.

It is dedicated to John Mendez, aka Silent Servant, Sumner’s dear friend and lifelong collaborator."

items.body:
In their sublime duo debut the simpatico synth & guitar of Jonny Nash & Tomo Katsurada is seduces to blissed, wind-whispering soundscapes, hashed out over the course of 12 months since Katsurada lent strings to Nash’s ‘Once Was Our Forever’. Dream material FFO Ghost, Makoto Kawabata, Joanne Robertson...

"Netherlands-based artists Tomo Katsurada (Ex-Kikagaku Moyo / Future Days Radio) and Jonny Nash (Melody As Truth) combine forces for an exploration into the sonic potential of the guitar duo, rooted in their experiences performing together over the last 12 months.

Friends and admirers of each other’s work for a decade, their musical collaboration began in 2024 with Katsurada asking Nash to contribute guitar to his debut EP ‘Dream Of The Egg’. Sensing the need to explore this further, they spent the following year performing together in different configurations, with Nash joining Katsurada’s trio and Katsurada in turn playing with Nash as a duo, across a wide spectrum of spaces, from churches and temples to concert halls, theatres and outdoor festivals. With new ideas developing organically out of these performances, recording new material became the next logical step. A short period of three days was set aside with a clear goal: to capture the essence of their fluid, intertwining melodies and guitar playing in a way that felt as direct and unfiltered as possible. Working from a handful of pre-existing sketches, they left ample room for experimentation to unfold within the process.

The results are presented on ‘At The Emerald Pool’, a collection of ten pieces that offer the listener a full immersion into the pair’s sound. With guitar as the primary instrument for both artists, it is no surprise that the core of the album lies here, specifically in the fluid interplay between the two players. Layers of gentle, delay-soaked fingerpicking often make it almost impossible to distinguish where one player ends and the other begins. As soloists, both Katsurada and Nash have a gift for crafting melodic lines that feel open and ascending, expressive and hopeful without becoming saccharine. Longer, more abstract pieces are counterbalanced by a series of shorter songs, with five vocal tracks appearing across the album. The decision to share vocal duties lends the record a unique quality and a strong sense of variation, bringing a wide expressive range out of a deliberately focused musical framework.

‘At The Emerald Pool’ represents the first chapter in an ongoing musical dialogue, an attempt to capture a moment of connection, openness and discovery, laying the foundation for what continues to unfold."

items.body:
New from Escho - 'Pusher' OST composer Peter Schneidermann (aka Peter Peter) taps his mates Majke Voss and Ice Age's Elias Rønnenfelt for his proper Bleeder debut, covering Lydia Lunch's 'Boy/Girl' and Fifty Foot Hose's 'If Not This Time' in the process.

Schneidermann is a familiar face on the Copenhagen scene, working closely with Nicolas Winding Refn on the 'Valhalla Rising' score as well as the scores for each of the 'Pusher' films. And he's been a member of the Escho family for years, so it was surely only a matter of time until he collaborated with Rønnenfelt. The band rush for the '90s on 'Marble Station', layering wall-of-sound guitars with deadpan vocals, while on 'Here Comes the Dead', they sound more like Black Country heroes Slade. The band's version of 'Boy/Girl' is stronger, led by rattling hi-hats and sleazy, Suicide-style guitars and they show off their range with their surprisingly tender version of 'If Not This Time'. It's all a bit knowing, sure, but it's Copenhagen, innit.

items.body:
Oren Ambarchi and Will Guthrie reconvene for a killer, fully tooled-up fusion of organ-esque Leslie vamps, sitar-style twangs and Guthrie's Han Bennink-inspired full kit theatrics - cover art of the year included.

Ambarchi and Guthrie are both so well established by now that they can do their thing completely free from the weight of expectation, and they've been working together for so long that they seem to fully operate on instinct. They know how it goes, they're just able to flex. And this set, recorded by Rabih Beaini and Filippo Samoré at Beaini's own Morphine Raum studio-cum-venue in Berlin before it was mixed and mastered a year later by Joe Talia, might be their best to date.

On the first side, they take it as slow as they like, with Ambarchi using his Leslie setup to transform his guitar into an organ, creating sustained notes that give Guthrie the space he needs to take the lead, landing on half rhythms and skeletal sequences for a moment before shifting to the next. It works like an establishing shot, building tension and making us wait for the pay off.

On the flip, it finally comes; Ambarchi's guitar is reshaped into a machine gun of harsh feedback resonances, angrily bowed into splintered riffs and sitar-like vibrations that shatter across the sonic spectrum. Guthrie works not just to fill in the gaps, but to provide momentum, swinging boldly from hushed pattern rolls to full, explosive jazz freakouts that anticipate Ambarchi's return to the Leslie. When Ambarchi starts plucking at the strings like a man possessed, coaxing out percussive staccato melodies that almost harmonise with Guthrie's cymbal bells, it all starts to slow down into wailing, woodwind-esque bird calls.

Heavy, heady biz from the best of the best...

Gorgeous DIY, private press, lounge jazz and Latin boogie stardust from 1984, framing keyboard maestro Ronald Langestraat in his living room, laying down pure vibes to 4-track - huge tip FFO Lewis, Gil Scott Heron, James Mason, Starship Commander Woooo Wooooo.

"Searching was self-recorded in Ronald’s living room on a 4-Track Tape Recorder in 1984. The recordings symbolise his engagement to cross-over everything that was known to him musically at that time. Most importantly, all recordings reflect his personal way of searching; searching for his own characteristic sound. Rhythmical patterns meet well balanced distortion, shaping the music into a mirror of his character. He was part of several Dutch Latin and Jazz bands, including Cascada and Ritmo Natural. With the latter he performed at Holland’s North Sea Jazz Festival. At this point Ronald is 78 years old, playing music every day.

Instruments: Acoustic Piano, Fender Rhodes Piano, Farfisa Organ, String Ensemble, Tenor Sax, Alt Sax, Soprano Sax, Clarinet, Alt Clarinet, Organ Bass, Micro Moog, Drums, Longa & Voices.”

items.body:
A decade since debuting as Ndagga Rhythm Force, Mark Ernestus’ incredible band draw on 100’s of hours studio and live practice for a staggering new suite of Senegalese x Berlin-styled mbalax steppers that prove, where needed, why they’re one of the best to do it right now. Absolutely exemplary, transcendent music for those that know.

Back at the start of the 2010s dub techno pioneer Mark Ernestus was spending a lot of time in Senegal, immersing in styles and patterns that historically underlined the reggae and dub musics he would heavily reference in his pivotal records made as Maurizio/Basic Channel/Rhythm & Sound, as co-produced with Moritz Von Oswald during the ‘90s and into the ’00s. 

In the process of researching and getting down to the roots of his passions, Ernestus encountered some of Senegal’s top tier musicians and recorded the Jeri-Jeri ensemble, revolving vocalist Mbene Diatta Seck and sabar drummer Bada Seck, and generating in 2013 the ‘800% Ndagga’ CD and its ’Ndagga Versions’ sibling, which better showcased Ernestus’ famed dub tekkerz inseparably woven into Senegalese music and the roots of myriad Afro-diasporic sounds.

That unit would morph into Ndagga Rhythm Force, producing an LP and trio of 12”s in 2015-2016 that set them on course to become one of the most impressive African bands on the contemporary gig circuit, throwing down live sets known to effortlessly go over 2 hours and propel so many legs and minds to new shapes and feels - trust they slay every time and should be top of all must-see lists.

With ‘Khadim’ Ndagga ditch their guitars and recalibrate a more lissom trio of voice and acoustic instruments bound with Ernestus’ Prophet 5 synth - the same model he’s relied upon since the Basic Channel days - on four extended songs that allow more light, space and emotion into a signature, rolling sound, centre-staging Mbene Seck’s husky diva croon over Bada Seck and Serigne Mamoune Seck’s dual, polymetric percussion, and judiciously juggled with Ernestus’ anti-gravity basses and plangent dub chord syncopation. 

In traditionally open-ended frameworks the quartet take all the time needed to stretch out and wrap heads into the tapestries of their storytelling grooves. A newfound atmospheric pressure and presence emerges in procession from the location recordings that fringe ‘Lamp Fall’ and its ode to a local mosque, reverberating in acres of implied space set by the ricocheting sabar drums and near-infrasonic subs, thru to the devotional depths of ’Nimzat’, rippling with thunderous chords and doleful ache. 

At its core are the LP’s most impressive parts; ‘Dieuw Bakhul’ uncoils a spellbinding Wolof tale of treachery to the rafters amid tempestuous chords that writhe stereo-wide with red-lining bite whilst drums knot sinuous, serpentine, to be resolved in the breathtaking 13’ steppers’ flight of ‘Khadim’, which lyrically hails Islam’s role in guiding Senegal to postcolonial times, spiritually meditates on bluest minor key riffs, and physically elevates bodies with aerodynamic finesse and hypnotic chronics kin to the best reggae and its offshoots. 

Deadly, soul and hoof gripping tunes. Do not miss!

The first three albums in the 'Everywhere At The End Of Time' series in one set - two and a half hours long, each album reveals new points of progression, loss and disintegration, falling further and further towards the abyss of complete memory loss and nothingness...

Embarking on the Caretaker’s final journey with the familiar vernacular of abraded shellac 78s and their ghostly waltzes to emulate the entropic effect of a mind becoming detached from everyone else’s sense of reality and coming to terms with their own, altered, and ever more elusive sense of ontology. The series aims to enlighten our understanding of dementia by breaking it down into a series of stages that provide a haunting guide to its progression, deterioration and disintegration and the way that people experience it according to a range of impending factors.

In other words, Everywhere At The End of Time probes some of the most important questions about modern music’s place in a world that’s increasingly haunted or even choked by the tightening noose of feedback loops of influence; perceptibly questioning the value of old memories as opposed to the creation of new ones, and, likewise the fidelity of those musical memories which remain, and whether we can properly recollect them from the mire of our faulty memory banks without the luxury of choice.
